Page title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/cleanup-untracked-table-folders
Meta description: Identify and optionally delete table folders that remain in object storage but are no longer tracked by the catalog.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- Cleanup Untracked Folders

On this page

# Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job

The Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job helps find table folders that still exist in object storage even though the corresponding tables are no longer active in the catalog.

Use this job when tables were dropped without purging their physical files. It can run in dry-run mode to report candidate folders, and it deletes folders only when deletion is explicitly enabled.

- Version: 0.1.5
- Source: View on GitHub

warning

This job can delete data from object storage. Always run it in dry-run mode first, review the candidates and audit table, and only enable deletion after confirming the output.

## Installation

You can deploy this job from the Marketplace or create the job template manually. The Marketplace flow is recommended because it pre-populates the image, main class, and default configuration.

### Marketplace

- Open Job Templates from the left sidebar.
- Click Marketplace to open the list of preconfigured Marketplace jobs.
- Find cleanup-untracked-table-folders, open the actions menu, and click Deploy.
- The Marketplace template opens a pre-filled Create New Job form. Review the defaults and update the configuration for your environment.

### Manual Setup

Create a job template manually with New Job Template if you do not use the Marketplace flow.

Specify the following parameters when creating the job manually:

| Field | Value

| Name | cleanup-untracked-table-folders

| Docker image | iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/cleanup-untracked-table-folders:0.1.5

| Main class | com.iomete.cleanup.untrackedtablefolders.App

| Main application file | spark-internal

| Config file path | /etc/configs/application.json

| Config file name | application.json

## Running the Job

The Marketplace template includes a default configuration under the Config Maps tab. Review the databases and safety settings before creating the job.

### Dry-Run Example

Use dry-run mode first to inspect candidates without deleting data.

```
{
  "catalog": "spark_catalog",
  "databases": ["analytics"],
  "exclude_paths": [],
  "exclude_database_folders": [],
  "older_than_hours": 24,
  "dry_run": true,
  "delete_enabled": false,
  "max_candidate_folders_per_database": 10
}

```

### Delete-Enabled Example

Enable deletion only after reviewing the dry-run output.

```
{
  "catalog": "spark_catalog",
  "databases": ["analytics"],
  "exclude_paths": [
    "s3a://bucket/data/analytics/protected_table"
  ],
  "exclude_database_folders": [],
  "older_than_hours": 24,
  "dry_run": false,
  "delete_enabled": true,
  "max_candidate_folders_per_database": 5
}

```

## Configuration Fields

| Field | Default | Description

| catalog | required | Catalog to inspect, for example spark_catalog.

| databases | required | List of database names to scan. The job does not scan all databases automatically.

| exclude_paths | [] | Full object-storage paths that must never be selected as candidates. Each entry must include a scheme and bucket, such as s3a://bucket/data/analytics/manual_archive; otherwise the job fails at startup.

| exclude_database_folders | [] | Database-relative folder exclusions in the format database.folder. The database must be listed in databases, and the folder must be an immediate child folder name without /.

| older_than_hours | 24 | A folder becomes a candidate only when the newest object inside it is at least this old.

| dry_run | true | Reports candidates without deleting data.

| delete_enabled | false | Must be true together with dry_run=false before deletion can happen. Setting dry_run=false without delete_enabled=true stops the job at startup.

| max_candidate_folders_per_database | 10 | Safety limit. If more candidates are detected for a database, the database is skipped.

| report_only_storage_roots | {} | Optional. Additional storage locations per database to list for review. Nothing in them is deleted. See Storage Roots.

| collect_size_statistics | ignored | Deprecated and ignored. Object count and size are always collected for candidate folders. You can remove this field.

Unknown fields in application.json are rejected at startup, so check the spelling of every field name.

## Recommended Workflow

- Run with dry_run=true and delete_enabled=false.
- Review the driver logs and audit table output.
- Check the STORAGE ROOTS section of the report and any partial_scan_coverage status for table locations the cleanup did not cover.
- Add exclude_paths or exclude_database_folders for anything that must be protected.
- Keep max_candidate_folders_per_database low for the first delete-enabled run.
- Enable deletion only after the dry-run output is reviewed.
- Query the audit table after the run.

## Safety Controls

The job is designed to fail closed. If it cannot prove that a path is safe to delete, it does not delete it.

| Safety check | Purpose

| dry_run=true by default | Reports candidates without deleting data.

| delete_enabled=false by default | Requires explicit confirmation before destructive cleanup.

| Explicit database list | Limits cleanup scope to configured databases.

| Scan-root validation | Prevents scanning outside the database storage boundary.

| Bucket-root and warehouse-root rejection | Never scans a database whose location is a bucket root, or equals or contains the catalog warehouse root, where other databases live.

| Supported storage only | Refuses databases on storage other than S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure storage.

| Active table protection | Protects folders that are active table locations, contain active table locations, or sit inside them.

| Other database protection | Protects storage of other databases visible in the catalog that sits inside the cleanup root.

| Iceberg write path protection | Protects folders named by an Iceberg table's write.*.path properties.

| Visible table anchor | Blocks deletion when no visible table is stored under the cleanup root.

| Pre-delete recheck | Re-discovers active table locations and write paths immediately before deletion, and stops if a table's storage can no longer be resolved.

| exclude_paths | Protects explicitly configured storage paths.

| exclude_database_folders | Protects database-relative folders without requiring full object-storage paths.

| Sentinel folder exclusion | Skips Spark/Hadoop staging folders such as _temporary and .spark-staging*.

| older_than_hours | Skips folders with recently written objects, and folders whose age cannot be established.

| max_candidate_folders_per_database | Skips cleanup when too many candidates are detected.

| Empty-database guard | Skips databases with no active table locations.

| Catalog-scoped storage access | Uses the selected catalog's own storage settings, and fails closed if they cannot be resolved.

| Unresolved ownership guard | Blocks deletion for a database when any table's storage location cannot be established.

| Audit integrity guard | Stops deleting for the rest of the run if an audit row cannot be written.

| Audit table | Records the outcome for each database.

## Object Storage Access

You do not configure storage settings or credentials for this job. Cleanup always uses the storage configuration associated with the catalog you selected in catalog.

If that storage configuration cannot be resolved safely, the job stops for that database and records FAILED. It does not fall back to any other storage configuration. This helps ensure cleanup remains within the storage associated with the selected catalog.

The job cleans databases stored on S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure storage. A database stored on another filesystem, such as HDFS, is skipped with status_reason=invalid_storage_location.

## Storage Roots

The job deletes folders only under one location per database, the cleanup root. It chooses the cleanup root from the database's table locations: when the tables share one parent folder, that folder is the cleanup root; otherwise the job uses the database location. The cleanup root must stay inside the database location, or the same path without the .db suffix.

When tables are stored under more than one parent folder, table locations outside the cleanup root are not checked in that run. The job reports them under TABLE LOCATIONS OUTSIDE THE SCANNED ROOT, and a successful audit row gets status_reason=partial_scan_coverage.

The job also lists other roots one level deep for review. Nothing in these report-only roots is ever deleted. A root is listed when it sits inside the database's own storage:

- the database location, or the same path without the .db suffix;
- for spark_catalog and IOMETE-managed REST catalogs, the catalog's namespace folder for the database;
- a location you approve in report_only_storage_roots, as long as at least one visible table of the database is stored under it.

```
{
  "report_only_storage_roots": {
    "sales": ["s3a://other-bucket/external/sales_events"]
  }
}

```

warning

Report-only roots are never deleted. A folder in a report-only root that is not matched to a visible table is not necessarily orphaned, because a table the job cannot see may own it. Approved report-only roots are not fully checked for ownership across databases.

Each key must be listed in databases. Approve only locations that belong to the database they are listed under. The job does not compare approved locations with the storage of other databases.

Other table parents are reported as not_scanned with a reason:

| Reason | Meaning

| outside_database_boundary | The parent is outside the database's own storage, in the same or another bucket.

| bucket_root | The parent is a bucket root.

| contains_warehouse_root | The parent equals or contains the catalog warehouse root.

| inside_table_location | The parent sits inside another table's folder.

| contains_database_storage | The location would contain the database's own location or namespace folder.

| no_visible_table | An approved location holds no visible table of the database.

| invalid_location | The location cannot be parsed.

| root_limit_reached | More than 25 additional roots were found; the rest are not listed.

Folders in report-only roots that do not belong to a visible table are listed under FOLDERS IN REPORT-ONLY ROOTS NOT MATCHED TO A VISIBLE TABLE. A table the job cannot see may still own them, so treat them as items to review, not as orphans.

## Excluding Paths

Use exclude_paths when you know the full object-storage path to protect. Each entry must include a scheme and bucket:

```
{
  "exclude_paths": [
    "s3a://bucket/data/analytics/manual_archive"
  ]
}

```

Use exclude_database_folders when you want to protect a folder relative to a configured database:

```
{
  "exclude_database_folders": [
    "analytics.manual_archive"
  ]
}

```

A folder is skipped when it equals an excluded path, contains one, or sits inside one. Paths are compared by whole path segments, so manual_archive does not protect manual_archive_v2. A database.folder exclusion also applies to the same folder name under every report-only root of that database.

Both forms are included in the effective excluded-path list written to the audit table.

## Other Databases and Iceberg Write Paths

Before choosing candidates, the job reads the location of every database it can see in the catalog. Storage of another database at or inside the cleanup root is protected and is never a candidate. On catalogs with many databases this step can take some time; the driver log reports how many databases were read and how long it took.

If the storage of other databases cannot be established, for example because a database location cannot be read, the database is BLOCKED with status_reason=other_database_storage_unknown and nothing is deleted.

For Iceberg tables, folders named by write.data.path, write.metadata.path, write.object-storage.path, and write.folder-storage.path are protected like the table location, both during candidate detection and in the pre-delete recheck.

## Audit Table

The job writes audit rows to:

```
spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.cleanup_untracked_table_folder_runs

```

Use the audit table to review candidates, skipped databases, deleted folders, runtime metadata, and failure details.

### Important Audit Columns

| Column | Meaning

| run_id | ID shared by all database rows from the same job execution.

| spark_app_id | Spark application ID for the job run.

| runtime_compute_id | Platform runtime compute/run identifier, when available.

| runtime_compute_namespace | Kubernetes namespace where the Spark driver ran, when available.

| runtime_domain | IOMETE domain from the runtime environment, when available.

| runtime_user | Spark runtime/run-as user from the driver environment, usually SPARK_USER.

| external_job_id | Stable platform Job ID shown in the UI, when exposed by the platform runtime.

| platform_started_by | Platform user who started this specific job run, when exposed by the platform runtime.

| catalog_name | Catalog scanned by the job.

| database_name | Database scanned by this audit row.

| operation | Cleanup operation name.

| dry_run | Whether the run was report-only.

| delete_enabled | Whether destructive deletion was explicitly enabled.

| older_than_hours | Age threshold used for candidate detection.

| cutoff_time | Timestamp cutoff derived from older_than_hours.

| max_candidate_folders_per_database | Candidate-count safety limit used for this run.

| excluded_paths | Effective excluded paths used during candidate detection.

| status | SUCCESS, SKIPPED, BLOCKED, or FAILED.

| status_reason | Machine-readable reason for skipped or failed outcomes.

| error_message | Error details for failed or intentionally skipped outcomes.

| discovered_database_location | Database location discovered from the catalog.

| storage_scan_location | Object-storage root scanned by the job.

| active_table_count | Number of active tables discovered for the database.

| unresolved_table_count | Number of tables whose storage location could not be read during discovery.

| storage_folder_count | Number of immediate storage folders discovered.

| candidate_folder_count | Number of folders confirmed as untracked and eligible for deletion.

| potentially_untracked_folder_count | Number of folders with no verified catalog owner, reported for review only when table storage ownership could not be fully verified.

| deleted_folder_count | Number of folders deleted.

| candidate_folders | Candidate folder paths.

| deleted_folders | Deleted folder paths.

| candidate_object_count | Estimated object count across candidate folders when size statistics are collected.

| candidate_total_size_bytes | Estimated candidate size when size statistics are collected.

| deleted_object_count | Object count for deleted folders when size statistics are collected.

| deleted_total_size_bytes | Deleted size when size statistics are collected.

| diagnostic_details | Additional contextual metadata for troubleshooting, such as path samples and truncation flags.

| start_time | Database processing start time.

| end_time | Database processing end time.

### Runtime Identity Fields

The audit table separates who the Spark job runs as, who started the run from the platform, and which platform job/run the audit row belongs to.

| Field | Example | Source | Meaning

| runtime_user | hasan | SPARK_USER from the driver environment | Spark runtime/run-as user. This is the user the Spark job executes as.

| platform_started_by | fde_admin | IOMETE_JOB_STARTED_BY, when exposed by the platform runtime | Platform user who started this specific run in the UI or platform backend. This can differ from runtime_user.

| external_job_id | 3e9342e7-89d3-42f8-a603-e00b783cca17 | IOMETE_EXTERNAL_JOB_ID, when exposed by the platform runtime | Stable platform Job ID for the job definition/template. This stays the same across multiple runs of the same job.

| runtime_compute_id | afceb977-cd1e-4ff8-89e3-2f7876436ecf | IOMETE_COMPUTE_ID, when available | Specific platform runtime/application identifier for one execution. This changes for each run.

| runtime_compute_namespace | spark-resources-1 | IOMETE_COMPUTE_NAMESPACE, when available | Kubernetes namespace where the Spark driver ran.

| runtime_domain | fde | IOMETE_DOMAIN, when available | IOMETE domain associated with the runtime.

| spark_app_id | spark-ffbd89771a0a4a248b947676b943557e | Spark application context | Spark application ID used to correlate with Spark logs/history.

| run_id | 2edb19ec-8cb0-4d27-8965-ffb4912bfa60 | Generated by this cleanup job | Cleanup job run ID. It groups all per-database audit rows from the same execution.

Example audit query:

```
SELECT
  start_time,
  database_name,
  status,
  status_reason,
  dry_run,
  delete_enabled,
  candidate_folder_count,
  deleted_folder_count,
  runtime_user,
  platform_started_by,
  external_job_id
FROM spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.cleanup_untracked_table_folder_runs
ORDER BY start_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

```

## Status Values

| Status | Description

| SUCCESS | The database was processed normally. Candidates may or may not have been found.

| SKIPPED | The job intentionally refused to process or delete for a safety reason.

| BLOCKED | Reconciliation completed far enough to inspect catalog and storage state, but a safety condition prevented cleanup. The findings are still reported.

| FAILED | An unexpected failure occurred while processing the database.

status_reason values:

| Status | Reason | Triggered when | What to check

| SUCCESS | partial_scan_coverage | Some table locations are outside the cleanup root, so storage around them was not checked. | Review TABLE LOCATIONS OUTSIDE THE SCANNED ROOT and STORAGE ROOTS in the report.

| SKIPPED | database_not_found | The configured database does not exist in the selected catalog. | Check the database name in databases and the catalog value.

| SKIPPED | database_location_missing | The catalog returns no storage location for the database. | Run DESCRIBE DATABASE EXTENDED and check its Location.

| SKIPPED | no_active_tables_in_database | No table in the database has a readable storage location, for example a database with no tables or only views. | Nothing to clean. If the database has tables, check them for unreadable locations.

| SKIPPED | too_many_candidate_folders | More candidate folders were found than max_candidate_folders_per_database allows, counted before the age check. | Review the candidate list in the audit row. Add exclusions or raise the limit only after review.

| SKIPPED | database_location_is_bucket_root | The database location is a bucket root. | The job cannot clean this database.

| SKIPPED | database_location_contains_warehouse_root | The database location equals or contains the catalog warehouse root, such as a default database at the warehouse root. | The job cannot clean this database.

| SKIPPED | catalog_warehouse_unknown | The selected catalog has no warehouse location configured. | Check the catalog's warehouse setting.

| SKIPPED | scan_root_outside_database_boundary | The folder that holds the database's tables is outside the database location. | Compare the table locations with the database location.

| SKIPPED | invalid_storage_location | The database or warehouse location has no scheme or bucket, a database, table, or warehouse location cannot be parsed, or the database is on unsupported storage such as HDFS. | Check that the locations are full URIs such as s3a://bucket/path on supported storage.

| BLOCKED | unresolved_catalog_ownership | At least one table's storage could not be established, so no folder in the database is deleted. | Check the tables under TABLES WHOSE STORAGE LOCATION COULD NOT BE RESOLVED and the reason logged for each. See Unresolved Table Storage Ownership.

| BLOCKED | cleanup_root_has_no_visible_table | No visible table is stored under the cleanup root. | Compare the table locations with the database location.

| BLOCKED | other_database_storage_unknown | The locations of other databases in the catalog could not be read or compared. | Check the driver log and the locations of the catalog's other databases. See Other Databases and Iceberg Write Paths.

| BLOCKED | audit_integrity_lost | An earlier audit write in the same run failed, so no more folders are deleted. | Check the driver log for the audit error and access to the audit table, then rerun.

| FAILED | deletion_failed | A folder could not be deleted, or a delete reported no change for a folder that still exists. Folders deleted before it stay deleted. | Check the folder named in diagnostic_details.deletion_failed_folder_path, when present, in object storage before the next run. See Partial Deletion and Audit Failures.

| FAILED | unexpected_error | Any other error while processing the database. | Check the driver log for the exception.

For databases skipped with database_location_is_bucket_root, database_location_contains_warehouse_root, or scan_root_outside_database_boundary, the job still lists report-only roots whose own checks pass and prints a STORAGE ROOT REPORT in the driver logs. Nothing is deleted.

## Partial Deletion and Audit Failures

Candidate folders are deleted one at a time. If a folder cannot be deleted, the job stops for that database and records FAILED with status_reason=deletion_failed.

- deleted_folder_count and deleted_folders list only the folders confirmed deleted before the failure, so they can be greater than zero on a FAILED row.
- diagnostic_details.deletion_failed_folder_path names the folder that failed. Check it in object storage before the next run.
- Other configured databases continue, as long as this database's audit row was written.

If an audit row cannot be written during a run, the job no longer has a reliable record of what it did. It deletes no more folders in that run, records later databases that would have been eligible for deletion as BLOCKED with status_reason=audit_integrity_lost, and fails at the end of the run. A database whose own audit row failed has no row in the audit table; use the driver log for that database.

## Unresolved Table Storage Ownership

A table is unresolved when it exists in the catalog but the job cannot establish which storage it owns. This includes a table whose Iceberg metadata, location, or properties cannot be read, a table with a missing or blank location (views excepted), a location without a scheme and bucket, an Iceberg table with gc.enabled set to anything but true or with write.location-provider.impl set, and an Iceberg write path that is blank or has no scheme and bucket. This does not mean the table is unhealthy or unwanted. It only means the job does not know which storage folder that table owns.

Storage reconciliation still runs and reports what it found. What changes is what the job is allowed to conclude. If any table in the database is unresolved, that table could own any of the unmatched folders, so no folder in that database can be proven untracked. For that database:

- Every unmatched folder is reported as potentially untracked, not as a candidate.
- potentially_untracked_folder_count carries those folders, and candidate_folder_count stays 0.
- Nothing is deleted, in dry-run mode or in deletion mode.
- The audit row is written with status=BLOCKED and status_reason=unresolved_catalog_ownership.

Other configured databases are unaffected and continue to run.

## Understanding Summary Logs

At the end of each database, the job prints a CLEANUP REPORT block in the driver logs. The header shows the run mode: Mode: dry run, nothing is deleted or Mode: deletion enabled. Its sections are:

| Report section | Source | Meaning

| CATALOG | Catalog metadata | Counts of tables found, tables with verified storage locations, and tables whose storage location could not be read.

| TABLES WHOSE STORAGE LOCATION COULD NOT BE RESOLVED | Catalog metadata | Tables that exist in the catalog but whose storage could not be established. Shown only when there are any.

| STORAGE | Object-storage scan | Counts of folders discovered under the cleanup root, folders belonging to verified catalog tables, folders protected or skipped for other reasons, and folders with no verified owner.

| STORAGE FOLDERS PROTECTED BY A VERIFIED CATALOG TABLE | Catalog metadata | Active table locations discovered from the catalog. These are the protection set and must not be deleted. This list may include paths outside the cleanup root.

| STORAGE FOLDERS EXCLUDED BY CONFIGURATION | Configuration | Paths protected by exclude_paths or exclude_database_folders.

| STORAGE FOLDERS PROTECTED OR SKIPPED FOR OTHER REASONS | Candidate detection | Folders that are excluded, belong to another database or an Iceberg write path, are framework working folders, or are too new or of unknown age. Shown only when there are any.

| TABLE LOCATIONS OUTSIDE THE SCANNED ROOT | Catalog metadata | Table locations outside the cleanup root. Storage around them was not checked in this run.

| STORAGE ROOTS | Object-storage scan | The cleanup root and report-only roots, with their status (scanned, absent, or listing_failed) and the roots that were not scanned.

| FOLDERS IN REPORT-ONLY ROOTS NOT MATCHED TO A VISIBLE TABLE | Object-storage scan | Folders in report-only roots that no visible table owns. These are never deleted.

| TABLE LOCATIONS OUTSIDE EVERY LISTED ROOT | Catalog metadata | Table locations that no listed root covers.

| UNTRACKED STORAGE FOLDERS | Candidate detection | Folders that were not protected and passed the cleanup filters. These are the folders the job would delete in deletion mode. When deletion is blocked, this section is titled UNTRACKED STORAGE FOLDERS (DELETION BLOCKED).

| POTENTIALLY UNTRACKED STORAGE FOLDERS | Candidate detection | Shown instead of the section above when a table's storage location could not be established. These folders have no verified catalog owner, but they cannot be proven untracked, so none of them are deletion candidates.

| DELETION | Deletion result | Folders actually deleted when dry_run=false and delete_enabled=true, Dry run. No folder was deleted. in dry-run mode, or BLOCKED with the reason when deletion was prevented.

In short, catalog active table locations come from catalog metadata, while storage folders come from the physical object-storage scan.

## Known Limitations

- Ownership is checked against the tables and databases the job can see in the catalog. A table or database the job cannot see does not protect its folder.
- Another database's table stored at a custom location inside the cleanup root is not protected.
- Files that an Iceberg table reaches without a write path property, for example through add_files, migrate, snapshot, or an earlier table location, are not protected.
- A Hive partition stored outside its table's folder is not protected.
- The job deletes whole untracked table folders, not individual orphan files inside active table folders.
- Folder names are compared case-sensitively, because ORDERS and orders are different object-storage prefixes.
- A database whose location equals or contains the catalog warehouse root cannot be cleaned by this job.
- Catalogs that use vended or remotely signed credentials are not supported for storage access.
- Folder age and size require listing every object in each candidate folder. This can take time for folders with many objects.

## Summary

Use this job to review and optionally clean table folders that remain in object storage after tables are no longer tracked by the catalog. Always start with dry-run mode, review the audit table, and enable deletion only after confirming that the candidates are safe to remove.

Page title: Data Compaction Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/data-compaction
Meta description: Keep Iceberg tables fast by running snapshot expiration, orphan file cleanup, data file compaction, and manifest rewrites on a schedule.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- Data Compaction

On this page

# Data Compaction Job

Iceberg tables slow down over time as small files, old snapshots, and unused files pile up. The Data Compaction Job cleans them up on a schedule. For every Iceberg table it processes, it runs four maintenance operations:

- Rewrite manifests: reorganizes table metadata for faster planning. See Rewrite Manifests.
- Rewrite data files: merges small files into larger ones. See Compact Data Files.
- Expire snapshots: removes old snapshots. See Expire Snapshots.
- Remove orphan files: deletes files no snapshot refers to. See Delete Orphan Files.

Tables in other formats, such as Hive or Parquet tables, are skipped.

tip

IOMETE also offers built-in Table Maintenance (beta), which runs these operations automatically when a table needs them. Use either the built-in feature or this job for a given table, not both.

- Version: 1.2.14 (see the Marketplace Jobs release notes for the latest version)
- Source: View on GitHub

## Installation

### Marketplace

Open Job Templates and click Marketplace. Find the data-compaction card, click the ⋮ menu, and select Deploy.

The job form opens pre-filled with recommended defaults and a weekly schedule. Review the config file (see Configuration), then click Create.

### Manual Setup

Open Job Templates in the sidebar and click New job template.

1. Name, Schedule, and Application

- Name: any name you like, for example data-compaction
- Schedule: select Cron and enter 0 12 * * 0 (every Sunday at 12:00). Use any cron expression that fits your needs. Without a schedule, the job only runs when you start it.
- Application type: Python
- Docker registry: default
- Docker image: iomete/iomete_data_compaction:1.2.14 (replace with the latest version)
- Main application file: local:///app/driver.py

2. Config File

Under Configurations, select the Config Maps tab and click Add config. Set File path to /etc/configs/application.conf and paste the HOCON template below.

```
{
    catalog: "spark_catalog",
    expire_snapshot: {
        retain_last: 1
    },
    rewrite_data_files: {
        options: {
            "min-input-files": 2,
            "target-file-size-bytes": 536870912
        }
    }
}

```

3. Instance Resources

Pick driver and executor instance types that fit the size of your tables.

Click Create to save the job.

## Configuration

The config file is HOCON. Only catalog is required. Every other field is optional and falls back to the default shown below.

### Choosing Tables

By default the job processes every table in every database of the catalog.

| Field | Default | Description

| catalog | required | The catalog to compact, for example spark_catalog.

| databases | [] | Databases to process. Empty means all databases in the catalog.

| table_include | [] | Tables to process. See the notes below.

| table_exclude | [] | Tables to skip.

Tables in table_include and table_exclude can be written as database.table to target one table, or as table to match that name in every database. Write table names in lowercase and without quotes, here and in table_overrides. A name that doesn't match a table is skipped without a warning.

warning

- table_include only limits the databases it mentions. Databases with no table in the list are still processed in full. To compact only a few tables, also set databases to just the databases those tables are in.
- If table_include is in the config at all, even as [], table_exclude is ignored. Leave table_include out when you use table_exclude.

### Operation Settings

Each operation has its own block. Set enabled: false in a block to skip that operation.

warning

With the default settings, each run keeps only the latest snapshot of every table. You cannot time travel to earlier versions, and long-running queries can fail. Set expire_snapshot.older_than_days or a higher retain_last if you need history. A snapshot is kept if it is one of the last retain_last snapshots, or if it is newer than older_than_days.

| Field | Default | Description

| expire_snapshot.enabled | true | Run snapshot expiration.

| expire_snapshot.retain_last | 1 | Always keep the N most recent snapshots.

| expire_snapshot.older_than_days | not set | Remove snapshots older than N days. When not set, any snapshot older than 5 minutes can be removed.

| remove_orphan_files.enabled | true | Run orphan file cleanup.

| remove_orphan_files.older_than_days | 1 | Only delete orphan files older than N days. Set this longer than your longest-running write, or files from a write still in progress can be deleted.

| rewrite_data_files.enabled | true | Run data file compaction.

| rewrite_data_files.strategy | binpack | binpack merges small files. sort also sorts rows, which is slower but can speed up queries.

| rewrite_data_files.sort_order | not set | Columns to sort by when strategy is sort, for example "user_id ASC, event_time DESC".

| rewrite_data_files.where | not set | Only compact rows that match this SQL filter, for example "date <= CURRENT_DATE - 1".

| rewrite_data_files.options | {} | Iceberg rewrite options such as min-input-files and target-file-size-bytes.

| rewrite_manifests.enabled | true | Run manifest rewrites.

### Other Settings

| Field | Default | Description

| parallelism | 4 | Number of tables processed at the same time.

| table_overrides | not set | Per-table operation settings. See Example 2.

| gc_handling.enabled | false | For tables with garbage collection turned off, turn it on for the run and off again afterwards. See the warning below.

| lock.enabled | false | Skip tables that another run is already compacting. See Table Locking.

| lock.ttl_seconds | 172800 | How long a lock lasts before it expires (48 hours).

danger

Leave gc_handling off unless you know why garbage collection was turned off on a table. Some tables, such as copies that share files with another table, have it off on purpose. Turning it on can delete files the other table still needs.

## Examples

### Example 1: Compact Selected Databases

Processes every table in analytics and production except production.raw_ingest.

```
{
    catalog: "spark_catalog",
    databases: ["analytics", "production"],
    table_exclude: ["production.raw_ingest"]
}

```

### Example 2: Different Settings for One Table

Keeps 7 days of snapshots everywhere, but 30 days for analytics.user_events, and rewrites that table sorted by user_id. rewrite-all rewrites every file, not just small ones, so the whole table ends up sorted.

```
{
    catalog: "spark_catalog",
    expire_snapshot: {
        older_than_days: 7
    },
    table_overrides: {
        analytics.user_events: {
            expire_snapshot: {
                older_than_days: 30
            },
            rewrite_data_files: {
                strategy: "sort",
                sort_order: "user_id ASC",
                options: {
                    "rewrite-all": true
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

```

### Example 3: Only Clean Up, No Rewrites

Expires snapshots and removes orphan files, but skips both rewrite operations.

```
{
    catalog: "spark_catalog",
    rewrite_data_files: {
        enabled: false
    },
    rewrite_manifests: {
        enabled: false
    }
}

```

## Table Locking

When lock.enabled is true, the job marks each table with the iomete.compaction.lock table property while it works on it. Other runs that also have lock.enabled set skip a table that is already locked. Runs without it ignore the lock, so turn it on in every job that compacts the same tables. The lock is removed when the table is done.

If a run crashes, its locks expire on their own after lock.ttl_seconds. To check or clear a lock by hand:

```
SHOW TBLPROPERTIES spark_catalog.analytics.user_events;

ALTER TABLE spark_catalog.analytics.user_events UNSET TBLPROPERTIES ('iomete.compaction.lock');

```

Set ttl_seconds longer than your slowest table takes to compact, or the lock can expire while the job is still working on it.

## Checking Results

A run can show as successful even when some tables failed, because the job continues with the next table. After a run, check these tables and the job's logs:

| Table | Contents

| spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.table_optimisation_run_metrics | Results of each operation on each table.

| spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.table_optimisation_run_errors | Tables where an operation failed, with the error.

## Running the Job

The Marketplace template runs every Sunday at 12:00. To trigger a run on demand, open the job and click Run.

To change the schedule, edit the job and set the Schedule parameter (cron expression).

Page title: File Streaming Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/file-streaming-job
Meta description: Continuously stream files from object storage into an Iceberg table with the File Streaming Spark job. Supports CSV, JSON, and Amazon S3 with SQS notifications.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- File Streaming

On this page

# File Streaming Job

The File Streaming Job continuously ingests files from object storage into an Iceberg table using Spark Structured Streaming. Point it at a source directory, or an SQS queue that notifies on new files, and it appends new files to the destination table on a fixed trigger interval.

- Version: 1.0.1
- Source: View on GitHub

## File Formats

- CSV
- JSON
- Amazon S3 with SQS notifications (s3-sqs), recommended for large or fast-growing buckets. See Amazon S3 with SQS.

## Installation

### Marketplace

Open Job Templates and click Marketplace. Find the file-streaming-job card, click the ⋮ menu, and select Deploy.

The Marketplace template opens a pre-filled Create New Job form. Review the source path and destination table in the config file (see Configuration) and update the values for your environment.

### Manual Setup

Open Streaming Jobs in the sidebar and click New Streaming Job if you do not use the Marketplace flow.

1. Name and Application

- Name: any name you like, for example file-streaming-job
- Application type: Python
- Docker image: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/iomete-file-streaming:1.0.1 (replace with the latest version)
- Main application file: local:///app/driver.py

2. Environment Variables

- LOG_LEVEL: INFO or ERROR

You can also use environment variables to store sensitive values, such as passwords or secrets, and reference them in your config file using the ${DB_PASSWORD} syntax.

3. Spark Config

- spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference: true

Set this when the config file doesn't provide an explicit schema for CSV. JSON and s3-sqs sources always need an explicit schema regardless of this setting. See Schema.

4. Config File

Expand Configurations, select the Config Maps tab, click Add config, and paste the HOCON template below. See Configuration for what each field does.

```
{
  source: {
    file: {
      format: csv,
      header: true,
      path: "s3a://bucket/path_to_csv_files/",
      max_files_per_trigger: 1,
      latest_first: false,
      max_file_age: "7d"
    }
  }
  destination: {
    schema: default,
    table: csv_file_stream,
    partitions: []
  }
  processing_time: {
    interval: 30,
    unit: seconds # minutes
  }
}

```

5. Instance Resources

Pick driver and executor instance types that fit your data volume.

Click Create to save the job.

## Configuration

The config file is HOCON. It declares the source, the destination table, and the streaming trigger interval.

### Source File

| Field | Description

| format | File format to read: csv or json (still used when source.queue is set, to tell the job how to parse the notified files). See Amazon S3 with SQS.

| header | Whether the CSV files include a header row (ignored when source.queue is set).

| path | Source directory path, including the filesystem scheme, for example s3a://bucket/path_to_csv_files/ (ignored when source.queue is set).

| max_files_per_trigger | Maximum number of new files to process per streaming trigger.

| latest_first | Whether to process the latest files first when there is a backlog (ignored when source.queue is set).

| max_file_age | Maximum age of files the stream considers, for example 7d.

| filename_only | Optional. Detect new files by filename only instead of full path. Only enable this if filenames are unique across the entire source; otherwise files with the same name in different folders are treated as duplicates and skipped.

### Destination

| Field | Description

| schema | Destination schema (database).

| table | Destination table.

| partitions | Optional. Destination partition columns.

### Processing Time

| Field | Description

| interval | Streaming trigger interval.

| unit | Trigger interval unit: seconds or minutes.

### Schema

CSV can infer its schema from the file (set spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference: true in Spark config) or use an explicit schema. JSON and s3-sqs sources always require an explicit schema; the job fails at startup with Schema must be defined. if one isn't provided.

Add schema under source to define one explicitly:

```
source: {
  schema: [
    { name: channel, type: string },
    { name: context, type: struct, properties: [
      { name: library, type: struct, properties: [
        { name: name, type: string },
        { name: version, type: string }
      ]}
    ]},
    { name: received_at, type: timestamp }
  ]
  file: { ... }
}

```

Supported type values:

- string
- int (or bigint/integer)
- double
- boolean
- date
- timestamp (or date-time/time)
- array (or list)
- struct, for nested fields, with its own properties

### Amazon S3 with SQS

Listing a source directory on every trigger gets expensive as a bucket grows. If an SQS queue is subscribed to S3 object-created notifications for the bucket, point the job at the queue instead of the directory.

Add queue under source. When queue is present, it takes over as the read path: the job still uses source.file.format to know how to parse the notified files, but source.file.path, header, and latest_first go unused.

```
source: {
  queue: {
    URL: "https://sqs.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/{account_number}/{queue_name}"
    fetch_interval_seconds: 2
    log_polling_wait_time_seconds: 5
  }
  schema: [
    { name: id, type: string }
  ]
  file: { ... }
}

```

source.file is still required even when queue is set; the job reads it unconditionally at startup. Set format to match your files (csv or json); path, header, and latest_first are ignored in this mode but the keys must still be present.

| Field | Description

| URL | SQS queue URL. The job parses the AWS region from this URL.

| fetch_interval_seconds | How often to poll the queue for new file notifications.

| log_polling_wait_time_seconds | Long-polling wait time for each SQS receive call.

note

schema is required when using the s3-sqs source. See Schema.

## Running the Job

Once deployed, the job runs continuously; there's no schedule to trigger. It reads new files as they arrive (or new SQS notifications, if configured) and appends them to the destination table on the configured processing_time interval.

# IOMETE Spark Jobs Marketplace

The Spark Jobs Marketplace gives you a library of pre-built jobs you can deploy in minutes instead of writing them from scratch. Browse All apps for built-in jobs covering ingestion, compaction, catalog sync, and more. Switch to My apps to publish your own job templates so others in your organization can discover and reuse them.

## Spark Jobs Marketplace

The Marketplace is where you'll find every built-in job IOMETE ships. Open the Job Templates page, then click Marketplace in the top-right corner.

## Available Jobs

Each card below links to a built-in job you can deploy today. Pick the one that matches your workload to see configuration details and examples.

For the latest version of each job, see the Marketplace Jobs release notes.

MySQL Database Replication Job

Move MySQL tables into the IOMETE Lakehouse with a simple, configuration-driven Spark job.

Query Scheduler Job

Schedule SQL queries to run in your data warehouse on a recurring cadence.

Data Compaction Job

Iceberg tables accumulate small files over time and slow down. This job compacts them on a per-table basis to keep performance healthy.

Lakehouse Backup Job

Back up and restore lakehouse files between S3-compatible object stores and HDFS-compatible storage.

Catalog Sync Job

Keep your data in sync with the Data Catalog so metadata stays accurate.

TPC-DS Generator Job

Generate TPC-DS datasets for benchmarking and performance evaluation.

Kafka to IOMETE Lakehouse Data Replication Job

A ready-to-use Spark Streaming job that replicates Kafka topics into the IOMETE Lakehouse through configuration alone.

File Streaming

A ready-to-use Spark Streaming job that replicates data from file sources (a directory, S3 location, and similar) into the IOMETE Lakehouse.

Page title: Kafka to Iceberg Streaming Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/kafka-iceberg-stream
Meta description: Stream data from Kafka topics into the IOMETE Lakehouse as Iceberg tables using a configuration-driven Spark Structured Streaming job.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- Kafka Streaming

On this page

# Kafka to Iceberg Streaming Job

The Kafka to Iceberg Streaming Job copies records from Kafka topics into an Iceberg table in the IOMETE Lakehouse using Spark Structured Streaming. Point it at a Kafka cluster and a topic pattern, and it continuously (or on a trigger) appends new records to the destination table.

- Version: 1.2.0
- Source: View on GitHub

## Deserialization Format

Only JSON deserialization is currently supported.

## Installation

### Marketplace

Open Job Templates and click Marketplace. Find the kafka-iceberg-stream card, click the ⋮ menu, and select Deploy.

The job form opens pre-filled with recommended defaults. Update the Kafka bootstrap servers, subscription pattern, and destination table in the config file (see Configuration Properties), then click Create.

### Manual Setup

Open Streaming Jobs in the sidebar and click New Streaming Job if you do not use the Marketplace flow.

1. Name and Application

- Name: any name you like, for example kafka-iceberg-stream
- Application type: Python
- Docker image: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/kafka-iceberg-stream:1.2.0 (replace with the latest version)
- Main application file: local:///app/job.py
- Java options (optional): -Dlog4j.configurationFile=/opt/spark/iomete/log4j2.properties, specify a logging configuration file

2. Config File

Expand Configurations, select the Config Maps tab, click Add config, and paste the HOCON template below. See Configuration Properties for what each field does.

```
{
  kafka: {
    options: {
      "kafka.bootstrap.servers": "kafka-bootstrap-server:9092",
      "subscribePattern": ".*"
    },

    # either once or processing_time should be set for the trigger. Not both.
    trigger: {
      # processing_time: "15 minutes",
      once: True
    },

    # set checkpoint_location to object storage for production.
    # Example: "s3a://assets-dir/checkpoints/kafka-streaming/data/app1"
    checkpoint_location: ".tmp/checkpoints/kafka-streaming/data/app1",
  },
  destination: {
    database: "default",
    table: "all_db_changes_v1",
  }
}

```

note

It's recommended to exclude the startingOffsets option. If the destination table doesn't exist or is empty, the job defaults to earliest automatically. If the table already has data, it defaults to latest. This lets the job start from the beginning on the first run and continue from where it left off (based on the checkpoint state) on every run after that.

3. Instance Resources

Pick driver and executor instance types that fit your throughput.

Click Create to save the job.

## Configuration Properties

| Field | Description

| kafka.options | Kafka consumer options, passed through as-is. See Kafka Consumer Configurations for the full list.

| kafka.trigger | Trigger options. See Triggers for details. Only one of processing_time or once may be set.

| kafka.checkpoint_location | Checkpoint location. See Checkpointing for details. Set this to object storage for production, for example s3a://assets-dir/checkpoints/kafka-streaming/data/app1.

| destination.database | Iceberg database name. The database must already exist.

| destination.table | Iceberg table name. The job creates the table if it doesn't exist.

The job creates the destination table with the following schema:

```
root
 |-- topic: string (nullable = true)
 |-- partition: integer (nullable = true)
 |-- offset: long (nullable = true)
 |-- timestamp: timestamp (nullable = true)
 |-- timestampType: integer (nullable = true)
 |-- key: string (nullable = true)
 |-- value: string (nullable = true)

```

| Column | Description

| topic | The Kafka topic the record was received from.

| partition | The Kafka partition the record was received from.

| offset | The Kafka offset of the record.

| timestamp | The Kafka timestamp of the record.

| timestampType | The Kafka timestamp type of the record.

| key | The Kafka record key.

| value | The Kafka record value.

## Running the Job

With trigger.once set, the job processes everything currently available on the topic and stops. Trigger it again (or run it on a schedule) to pick up new records. With trigger.processing_time set, the job runs continuously, checking for new records at the given interval.

To trigger a run on demand, open the job and click Run.

Page title: Lakehouse Backup Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/lakehouse-backup
Meta description: Back up and restore lakehouse files between S3-compatible object stores and HDFS-compatible storage with a Spark job.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- Lakehouse Backup

On this page

# Lakehouse Backup Job

The Lakehouse Backup Job copies all files and folders under a configured storage path between S3-compatible object stores and HDFS-compatible storage. It preserves relative paths and runs file copies in parallel across a Spark cluster, so you can use the same job for scheduled backups and restores.

- Image: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/iomete-lakehouse-backup:<VERSION>
- Latest version: Marketplace Jobs release notes
- Source: View on GitHub

warning

The job copies files as they exist during the run. It does not create a transactionally consistent snapshot while applications continue writing to the source. Run the backup when the source is not changing.

## Supported Storage Paths

You can configure either storage type as the source or target.

| Source | Target | Typical use

| S3 | S3 | Copy data to another bucket, account, region, or S3-compatible system.

| S3 | HDFS | Back up object-store data to Dell Isilon, OneFS, or Hadoop storage.

| HDFS | S3 | Restore or migrate HDFS data to object storage.

| HDFS | HDFS | Copy data between HDFS-compatible systems.

S3 support includes AWS S3 and compatible systems such as Dell ECS and Ceph. HDFS support uses simple authentication and works with systems such as Dell Isilon, OneFS, and Hadoop clusters.

## Creating the Job Template

Before you create the job, make sure the source credentials allow reads and the target credentials allow writes. For HDFS, the Spark driver and executors must be able to reach the NameNode and every DataNode.

Open Job Templates and click New Job Template. See Creating a Spark Job for a walkthrough of the job form.

Configure the application:

| Field | Value

| Docker image | iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/iomete-lakehouse-backup:<VERSION>

| Main application file | spark-internal

| Main class | com.iomete.backup.App

| Arguments | /etc/configs/application.json

Replace <VERSION> with the version listed in the Marketplace Jobs release notes.

Choose an instance size for the amount of data you need to copy.

Under Configurations → Config Maps, add a file with the path /etc/configs/application.json, then paste your configuration. See Config Maps for details.

Add each credential as an environment variable whose name matches the ${VAR_NAME} value in the JSON. Set its value from an IOMETE Secret (recommended).

Add a schedule if you want the backup to run automatically, then create the job.

The selected instance normally supplies the executor count and CPU settings. If either value is missing, the run fails before copying data and reports the Spark setting you need to add: spark.kubernetes.executor.limit.cores and either spark.executor.instances or spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors.

## Configuring an S3-to-S3 Backup

Use separate source and target credentials when the locations belong to different accounts or systems.

```
{
  "source": {
    "type": "s3",
    "bucket": "<SOURCE_BUCKET>",
    "prefix": "<SOURCE_PREFIX>",
    "accessKey": "${SOURCE_ACCESS_KEY}",
    "secretKey": "${SOURCE_SECRET_KEY}"
  },
  "target": {
    "type": "s3",
    "bucket": "<TARGET_BUCKET>",
    "prefix": "<TARGET_PREFIX>",
    "accessKey": "${TARGET_ACCESS_KEY}",
    "secretKey": "${TARGET_SECRET_KEY}"
  }
}

```

Replace the bucket and prefix placeholders with your storage locations. The job copies every source file under SOURCE_PREFIX to the same relative path under TARGET_PREFIX.

For a non-AWS S3-compatible system, add its endpoint and enable path-style access when the system requires it:

```
{
  "type": "s3",
  "bucket": "lakehouse-backup",
  "prefix": "production",
  "endpoint": "https://object-storage.example.com",
  "pathStyleAccess": true,
  "accessKey": "${S3_ACCESS_KEY}",
  "secretKey": "${S3_SECRET_KEY}",
  "region": "us-east-1"
}

```

### S3 Configuration

| Field | Required | Default | Description

| type | Yes | — | Set to s3.

| bucket | Yes | — | S3 bucket name.

| prefix | No | Empty | Folder prefix under the bucket.

| endpoint | No | AWS default | Endpoint for an S3-compatible system.

| pathStyleAccess | No | false | Uses path-style bucket addressing when set to true.

| accessKey | Yes | — | Access key, normally provided through an IOMETE Secret.

| secretKey | Yes | — | Secret key, normally provided through an IOMETE Secret.

| region | No | us-east-1 | S3 region.

## Configuring HDFS Storage

Use an HDFS block as either source or target. This example backs up S3 data to HDFS:

```
{
  "source": {
    "type": "s3",
    "bucket": "<SOURCE_BUCKET>",
    "prefix": "<SOURCE_PREFIX>",
    "accessKey": "${SOURCE_ACCESS_KEY}",
    "secretKey": "${SOURCE_SECRET_KEY}"
  },
  "target": {
    "type": "hdfs",
    "namenode": "isilon.example.com:8020",
    "path": "backups/lakehouse",
    "user": "iomete-backup"
  }
}

```

For Dell Isilon or OneFS, use the SmartConnect zone FQDN for namenode so connections can be balanced across nodes.

| Field | Required | Default | Description

| type | Yes | — | Set to hdfs.

| namenode | Yes | — | NameNode RPC endpoint in host:port format.

| path | No | Empty | Directory under the filesystem root.

| user | Yes | — | HDFS user with the required read or write permissions.

| authentication | No | simple | Authentication mode. Only simple is supported.

Simple authentication uses the configured user name without a password. Kerberos-secured HDFS clusters are not supported.

## Configuring Copy Behavior

The default copy settings work for most backups. Add a copy block when you need timestamped backup folders, a full copy, a bandwidth limit, or different performance settings.

```
{
  "copy": {
    "skipIdentical": true,
    "targetTimestampFolder": "daily",
    "clockSkewToleranceMs": 30000,
    "slotsPerVcpu": 4,
    "tasksPerSlot": 20,
    "perFileOverheadBytes": 26214400,
    "maxBytesPerTask": 1073741824,
    "maxBandwidthMbPerSec": 600
  }
}

```

| Field | Default | Description

| skipIdentical | true | Skips a target file when its size matches and its modification time is sufficiently newer than the source. Set to false to copy every source file.

| targetTimestampFolder | Unset | Adds an hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly UTC folder under the target path. Unset writes directly to the target path.

| clockSkewToleranceMs | 30000 | Required target timestamp margin when deciding whether a file is identical.

| slotsPerVcpu | 4 | Maximum concurrent file copies per executor vCPU.

| tasksPerSlot | 20 | Target number of Spark tasks per copy slot.

| perFileOverheadBytes | 26214400 | Estimated fixed per-file cost used to balance tasks. It does not add bytes to the copy.

| maxBytesPerTask | 1073741824 | Maximum estimated work assigned to a normal task. A larger individual file remains whole in its own task.

| maxBandwidthMbPerSec | Unset | Maximum aggregate copy rate across the whole job in MB/s. Unset means uncapped.

The job does not split individual files. It stages each write under a temporary target path, verifies that the written length matches the source, and then renames the file into place. It retries temporary failures and fails the run if any file cannot be copied. Files that exist only at the target are not deleted.

### Creating Timestamped Backup Folders

By default, every run copies files to the target path in your configuration. Changed files replace their existing copies, while files deleted from the source remain at the target.

Set targetTimestampFolder when you want a separate target folder for each hour, day, week, or month. This example creates one folder per day:

```
{
  "copy": { "targetTimestampFolder": "daily" }
}

```

If a run starts on February 14, 2026, the job appends 2026-02-14 to the configured target path. Folder names use the run start time in UTC:

| Value | Folder example

| hourly | 2026-02-14-09

| daily | 2026-02-14

| weekly | 2026-W07

| monthly | 2026-02

All runs that start in the same period use the same folder. For example, every daily run started on February 14 writes to 2026-02-14. When skipIdentical is enabled, later runs skip files that are already present and unchanged, then copy only new or changed files.

note

The job does not delete old timestamped folders or files that no longer exist at the source. Use a storage lifecycle rule or a separate cleanup job to remove them.

## Recording Run History

Run-history recording is enabled by default. The job creates these Iceberg tables on its first run:

| Table | Contents

| spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.lakehouse_backup_runs | One row per run with status, counts, byte totals, stage timings, and copy settings.

| spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.lakehouse_backup_run_file_failures | One row per recorded file failure, joined by run_id.

To disable recording, change its database, or limit recorded failure rows, add a stats block:

```
{
  "stats": {
    "enabled": true,
    "database": "spark_catalog.iomete_system_db",
    "maxFailureRows": 1000
  }
}

```

| Field | Default | Description

| enabled | true | Records run history when enabled.

| database | spark_catalog.iomete_system_db | Database for both history tables. You can include or omit the catalog.

| maxFailureRows | 1000 | Maximum failure details stored for one run. The run table still records the full failure count.

A history-table write failure produces a warning but does not turn a successful backup into a failed run.

## Running and Checking a Backup

- Confirm that applications are not changing the source files.
- Open the job template and start a run.
- Monitor the run as described in Running a Spark Job.
- After it finishes, query the run-history table:

```
SELECT run_id,
       status,
       started_at,
       ended_at,
       files_copied,
       files_skipped,
       files_failed,
       bytes_copied,
       error_message
FROM spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.lakehouse_backup_runs
ORDER BY started_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

```

A complete backup has status = 'SUCCEEDED', files_failed = 0, and a populated ended_at. A run that remains RUNNING long after it started usually means its driver stopped before recording the outcome.

To inspect failed files, replace <RUN_ID> and run:

```
SELECT source_path, target_path, attempts_used, error
FROM spark_catalog.iomete_system_db.lakehouse_backup_run_file_failures
WHERE run_id = '<RUN_ID>'
ORDER BY source_path;

```

## Restoring a Backup

Create a separate job template for restores so a scheduled backup cannot accidentally run with reversed locations. Configure the backup location as source and the restore location as target, then run it while the restore target is not being written by another process.

For example, restore an HDFS backup to S3 with:

```
{
  "source": {
    "type": "hdfs",
    "namenode": "isilon.example.com:8020",
    "path": "backups/lakehouse",
    "user": "iomete-backup"
  },
  "target": {
    "type": "s3",
    "bucket": "<RESTORE_BUCKET>",
    "prefix": "<RESTORE_PREFIX>",
    "accessKey": "${RESTORE_ACCESS_KEY}",
    "secretKey": "${RESTORE_SECRET_KEY}"
  }
}

```

After the run succeeds, validate the restored catalog or workload against the copied files before directing production traffic to it.

## Tuning Copy Performance

Start with the defaults and compare successful runs of the same source before changing anything. The run-history table separates source listing, target listing, planning, copy, and directory-creation time, and it records effective concurrency and task shape.

- Raise slotsPerVcpu only when copy slots stay busy and additional concurrency continues to improve throughput.
- Raise tasksPerSlot when too few tasks leave slots idle near the end of the copy.
- Raise perFileOverheadBytes when tasks containing many small files run much longer than others.
- Set maxBandwidthMbPerSec when the backup must leave network capacity for other workloads.

For the full metrics reference and tuning queries, see Backup run history. To benchmark controlled configuration changes in your environment, follow the load-testing runbook.

Page title: MySQL Database Replication Job | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/open-source-spark-jobs/mysql-db-sync
Meta description: Replicate MySQL tables to the IOMETE Lakehouse with a configuration-driven Spark job. Supports full load and incremental snapshot sync modes.

---

- Open Source Spark Jobs
- MySQL Database Replication

On this page

# MySQL Database Replication Job

The MySQL Database Replication Job copies tables from a MySQL database into the IOMETE Lakehouse on a schedule. You point the job at a source database, list the tables to sync, choose between a full reload or an incremental snapshot, and the job handles the rest.

- Version: see the Marketplace Jobs release notes for the latest version
- Source: View on GitHub

## Installation

### Marketplace

Open Job Templates and click Marketplace. Find the mysql-sync card, click the ⋮ menu, and select Deploy.

The job form opens pre-filled with recommended defaults. Add your database password as an environment variable and your sync rules as a config file (see Configuration), then click Create.

tip

To customize the template, copy it from the Marketplace into your own job and adjust as needed.

### Manual Setup

Open Job Templates in the sidebar and click New Job Template.

1. Name and Application

- Name: any name you like, for example mysql-db-sync
- Application type: Python
- Docker image: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/iomete_mysql_sync:<version> (see Marketplace Jobs release notes for the latest version)
- Main application file: local:///app/driver.py

2. Environment Variables

Store the database password as an environment variable rather than checking it into the config file. Add a variable named DB_PASSWORD with your MySQL password as the value, then reference it from the config as ${DB_PASSWORD}.

3. Config File

Expand Application configurations, click Add config file, and paste the HOCON template below. See Configuration for what each field does.

```
{
    source_connection: {
        host: "your-mysql-host.example.com",
        port: 3306,
        username: mysql_user,
        password: $\{DB_PASSWORD}
    },
    syncs: [
        {
            source.schema: employees
            source.tables: ["*"]
            source.exclude_tables: [departments, dept_manager]
            destination.schema: employees_raw
            sync_mode.type: full_load
        }
    ]
}

```

4. Instance Resources

Pick driver and executor instance types that fit your data volume.

Click Create to save the job.

## Configuration

The config file is HOCON. It declares the source MySQL connection and one or more sync entries.

### Source Connection

| Field | Description

| host | The address of the MySQL database, for example your-mysql-host.example.com.

| port | The MySQL port, usually 3306.

| username | The MySQL user the job connects as.

| password | The user's password. Reference an environment variable like ${DB_PASSWORD} rather than embedding the value.

### Syncs

The syncs array contains one or more sync entries. Each entry describes a source schema, the tables to include, the destination schema in IOMETE, and the sync mode.

| Field | Description

| source.schema | The schema in the MySQL database to read from.

| source.tables | The tables to sync. Use ["*"] to include every table in the schema. You can also pass a SQL subquery as a virtual table — see Subquery Sources.

| source.exclude_tables | Optional. Tables to skip when source.tables is ["*"].

| destination.schema | The schema in the IOMETE Lakehouse where rows are written.

| sync_mode.type | Either full_load or incremental_snapshot. See Sync Modes.

### Sync Modes

#### full_load

Reads everything from the source table and overwrites the destination table on every run. Use this for small or slowly-changing tables where you want each run to be a clean snapshot.

#### incremental_snapshot

Brings over only rows inserted or updated since the last run, using a MERGE statement against a snapshot of the table in the destination. Use this for large tables where a full reload is too expensive.

This mode requires two extra fields:

| Field | Description

| sync_mode.identification_column | The primary key column used in the merge condition, typically id.

| sync_mode.tracking_column | A monotonically increasing column the job uses to find new rows since the last sync, typically updated_at. The column must be set on every insert and update.

### Subquery Sources

Instead of a table name, an entry in source.tables can be a SQL subquery wrapped in triple-quoted HOCON strings, with an alias. This replicates a derived view rather than a raw table.

```
source.tables: [
  """
  (SELECT emp_no, sum(salary) total_salary FROM salaries group by emp_no)
  as total_salaries
  """
]

```

The job replicates the subquery result into a destination table named after the alias (total_salaries in this example).

## Examples

### Example 1: Full Load Excluding Some Tables

Replicates every table in the employees schema except salaries into employees_raw on each run.

```
{
    source.schema: employees
    source.tables: ["*"]
    source.exclude_tables: [salaries]
    destination.schema: employees_raw
    sync_mode.type: full_load
}

```

### Example 2: Specific Tables Full Load

Replicates only the departments and dept_manager tables.

```
{
    source.schema: employees
    source.tables: [departments, dept_manager]
    destination.schema: employees_raw
    sync_mode.type: full_load
}

```

### Example 3: Incremental Snapshot

Brings over only new or changed rows in the salaries table, using id as the primary key and updated_at as the change-tracking column.

```
{
    source.schema: employees
    source.tables: [salaries]
    destination.schema: employees_raw
    sync_mode: {
      type: incremental_snapshot
      identification_column: id
      tracking_column: updated_at
    }
}

```

## Running the Job

The job runs on its schedule. To trigger a run on demand, open the job and click Run.

To change the schedule, edit the job and set the Schedule parameter (cron expression).

# Query Scheduler Job

IOMETE provides Query Scheduler Job to run your warehouse queries on a schedule or manually.

### Installation

- In the left sidebar, under Applications, click Job Templates.
- Click Marketplace to open the list of preconfigured Marketplace jobs.
- Find query-scheduler-job, open the actions menu, and click Deploy.
- The Marketplace template opens a pre-filled Create New Job form. Review the defaults and update the values for your environment.

You can also create a job template manually with New Job Template, but the Marketplace flow is recommended because it pre-populates the Query Scheduler image, schedule, environment variables, and default query configuration.

Specify the following parameters (these are examples, you can change them based on your preference):

- Name: query-scheduler-job
- Schedule: 0 0/22 1/1 * *
- Docker image: iomete/spark-py:3.5.7-v1
- Main application file: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/query-scheduler-job/main/job.py
- Environment variables: LOG_LEVEL: INFO

### Environment variables

The Marketplace template includes LOG_LEVEL by default.

### Config file

- Config file: The Marketplace template includes a default query configuration under the Config Maps tab. Review the queries and update them for your environment.

```
# Queries to be run sequentially
[
  # let's create an example SELECT
  """
  SELECT 1
  """
]

```

Click Create after reviewing the job configuration.

## Summary

You can find the source code in GitHub. Feel free to customize the code for your requirements. Please contact us if you have any questions.

The job runs according to the cron schedule after it is created. To run it manually, use a one-time schedule when creating the job, or create the job first and then trigger it from the job list with the Run action.

Page title: Manage, Create and Manage Iceberg Tables Using DDL | IOMETE
URL: https://iomete.com/resources/reference/iceberg-tables/ddl
Meta description: Data definition language is a syntax for creating and modifying database objects such as tables, indices, and users

---

- Iceberg Tables
- DDL

On this page

# Manage, Create and Manage Iceberg Tables Using DDL

### CREATE TABLE

```
CREATE TABLE sample (id bigint COMMENT 'unique id', data string);

```

Iceberg will convert the column type in Spark to the corresponding Iceberg type. Please check the section of type compatibility on creating table for details.

Table create commands, including CTAS and RTAS, support the full range of Spark create clauses, including:

- PARTITION BY (partition-expressions) to configure partitioning
- LOCATION '(fully-qualified-uri)' to set the table location
- COMMENT 'table documentation' to set a table description
- TBLPROPERTIES ('key'='value', ...) to set table configuration

### PARTITIONED BY

To create a partitioned table, use PARTITIONED BY:

```
CREATE TABLE sample ( id bigint, data string, category string) PARTITIONED BY (category)

```

The PARTITIONED BY clause supports transform expressions to create hidden partitions.

```
CREATE TABLE sample (
    id bigint,
    data string,
    category string,
    ts timestamp)
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(16, id), days(ts), category)

```

Supported transformations are:

- years(ts): partition by year
- months(ts): partition by month
- days(ts) or date(ts): equivalent to dateint partitioning
- hours(ts) or date_hour(ts): equivalent to dateint and hour partitioning
- bucket(N, col): partition by hashed value mod N buckets
- truncate(L, col): partition by value truncated to L

- Strings are truncated to the given length
- Integers and longs truncate to bins: truncate(10, i) produces partitions 0, 10, 20, 30, …

### CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT

```
CREATE TABLE sample
AS SELECT ...

```

### REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT

Atomic table replacement creates a new snapshot with the results of the SELECT query, but keeps table history.

```
REPLACE TABLE sample
AS SELECT ...

```

```
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE sample
AS SELECT ...

```

caution

The schema and partition spec will be replaced if changed. To avoid modifying the table’s schema and partitioning, use INSERT OVERWRITE instead of REPLACE TABLE. The new table properties in the REPLACE TABLE command will be merged with any existing table properties. The existing table properties will be updated if changed else they are preserved.

### DROP TABLE

To delete a table, run:

```
DROP TABLE sample

```

## ALTER TABLE

Full ALTER TABLE support:

- Renaming a table
- Setting or removing table properties
- Adding, deleting, and renaming columns
- Adding, deleting, and renaming nested fields
- Reordering top-level columns and nested struct fields
- Widening the type of int, float, and decimal fields
- Making required columns optional

### ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO

```
ALTER TABLE sample RENAME TO new_name

```

### ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES

```
ALTER TABLE sample SET TBLPROPERTIES (
    'read.split.target-size'='268435456'
)

```

Iceberg uses table properties to control table behavior. For a list of available properties, see Table configuration.

UNSET is used to remove properties:

```
ALTER TABLE sample UNSET TBLPROPERTIES ('read.split.target-size')

```

### ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN

To add a column use the ADD COLUMNS clause with ALTER TABLE:

```
ALTER TABLE sample
ADD COLUMNS (
    new_column string comment 'new_column docs'
 )

```

Multiple columns can be added at the same time, separated by commas.

Nested columns should be identified using the full column name:

```
-- create a struct column
ALTER TABLE sample
ADD COLUMN point struct<x: double, y: double>;

-- add a field to the struct
ALTER TABLE sample
ADD COLUMN point.z double

```

You can add columns in any position by adding FIRST or AFTER clauses:

```
ALTER TABLE sample
ADD COLUMN new_column bigint AFTER other_column

```

```
ALTER TABLE sample
ADD COLUMN nested.new_column bigint FIRST

```

### ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN

To rename a field, use RENAME COLUMN:

```
ALTER TABLE sample RENAME COLUMN data TO payload
ALTER TABLE sample RENAME COLUMN location.lat TO latitude

```

Note that nested rename commands only rename the leaf field. The above command renames location.lat to location.latitude

### ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN

Alter column is used to widen types, make a field optional, set comments, and reorder fields.

Iceberg allows updating column types if the update is safe. Safe updates are:

- int to bigint
- float to double
- decimal(P,S) to decimal(P2,S) when P2 > P (scale cannot change)

```
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN measurement TYPE double

```

To add or remove columns from a struct, use ADD COLUMN or DROP COLUMN with a nested column name.

Column comments can also be updated using ALTER COLUMN:

```
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN measurement TYPE double
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN measurement COMMENT 'unit is bytes per second'
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN measurement COMMENT 'unit is kilobytes per second'

```

Iceberg allows reordering top-level columns or columns in a struct using FIRST and AFTER clauses:

```
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN col FIRST

```

```
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN nested.col AFTER other_col

```

Nullability can be changed using SET NOT NULL and DROP NOT NULL:

```
ALTER TABLE sample ALTER COLUMN id DROP NOT NULL

```

Note

ALTER COLUMN is not used to update struct types. Use ADD COLUMN and DROP COLUMN to add or remove struct fields.

### ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN

To drop columns, use ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN:

```
ALTER TABLE sample DROP COLUMN id
ALTER TABLE sample DROP COLUMN point.z

```

### ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION FIELD

Add new partition fields to a spec using ADD PARTITION FIELD:

```
ALTER TABLE sample ADD PARTITION FIELD catalog -- identity transform

```

Partition transforms are also supported:

```
ALTER TABLE sample ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, id)
ALTER TABLE sample ADD PARTITION FIELD truncate(4, data)
ALTER TABLE sample ADD PARTITION FIELD year(ts)
-- use optional AS keyword to specify a custom name for the partition field
ALTER TABLE sample ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, id) AS shard

```

Adding a partition field is a metadata operation and does not change any of the existing table data. New data will be written with the new partitioning, but existing data will remain in the old partition layout. Old data files will have null values for the new partition fields in metadata tables.

info

To migrate from daily to hourly partitioning with transforms, it is not necessary to drop the daily partition field. Keeping the field ensures existing metadata table queries continue to work.

caution

Dynamic partition overwrite behavior will change when partitioning changes For example, if you partition by days and move to partitioning by hours, overwrites will overwrite hourly partitions but not days anymore."

### ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION FIELD

Partition fields can be removed using DROP PARTITION FIELD:

```
ALTER TABLE prod.db.sample DROP PARTITION FIELD catalog
ALTER TABLE prod.db.sample DROP PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, id)
ALTER TABLE prod.db.sample DROP PARTITION FIELD truncate(4, data)
ALTER TABLE prod.db.sample DROP PARTITION FIELD year(ts)
ALTER TABLE prod.db.sample DROP PARTITION FIELD shard

```

Note that although the partition is removed, the column will still exist in the table schema.

Dropping a partition field is a metadata operation and does not change any of the existing table data. New data will be written with the new partitioning, but existing data will remain in the old partition layout.

caution

Dynamic partition overwrite behavior will change when partitioning changes For example, if you partition by days and move to partitioning by hours, overwrites will overwrite hourly partitions but not days anymore.

caution

Be careful when dropping a partition field because it will change the schema of metadata tables, like files, and may cause metadata queries to fail or produce different results.

### ALTER TABLE ... WRITE ORDERED BY

Iceberg tables can be configured with a sort order that is used to automatically sort data that is written to the table in some engines. For example, MERGE INTO in Spark will use the table ordering.

To set the write order for a table, use WRITE ORDERED BY:

```
ALTER TABLE sample WRITE ORDERED BY category, id
-- use optional ASC/DEC keyword to specify sort order of each field (default ASC)
ALTER TABLE sample WRITE ORDERED BY category ASC, id DESC
-- use optional NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST keyword to specify null order of each field (default FIRST)
ALTER TABLE sample WRITE ORDERED BY category ASC NULLS LAST, id DESC NULLS FIRST

```

info

Table write order does not guarantee data order for queries. It only affects how data is written to the table.

IOMETE

Run Spark and Iceberg on your own infrastructure

IOMETE is a self-hosted data lakehouse: SQL, Spark jobs, streaming and notebooks on Apache Iceberg. It runs on your own Kubernetes, on-premises, in your cloud account or air-gapped.

Book a demoTry the free plan →
